steps.title: Đọc
steps.heading: Is automation a threat or an opportunity?
steps.purpose: Đọc để tìm: tác giả mô tả thị trường lao động thay đổi thế nào, và dùng bằng chứng gì?
text: Few developments have unsettled the modern workplace as profoundly as automation. According to the World Economic Forum, roughly 22 per cent of today's jobs will be disrupted by 2030, with some 170 million new roles created and 92 million displaced. These headline figures conceal a harder truth: job displacement does not affect everyone equally. Behind each percentage lies a person deciding whether to retrain, relocate or wait.

Consider the labour market itself. Rarely have employers complained so loudly of a skills gap while, at the same time, thousands of experienced staff face redundancy. Both problems coexist because the tasks that disappear are not usually the tasks that new vacancies require. A clerk whose work has been automated cannot become a data analyst overnight. The World Economic Forum even names the skills gap as the most significant obstacle to business transformation, a finding that employers would do well to take seriously.

The rise of the gig economy has complicated matters further. Younger workers are often drawn to such arrangements, whereas older colleagues tend to value stability. Not only does the model offer flexibility to those who want it, but it also leaves many people without sick pay, pensions or any formal protection. Once a firm restructures, a casual workforce can shrink within days, and even a long-serving employee may be made redundant. Never before has the pace of change been so fast, nor has so much depended on how societies respond.

box.title: Ghi nhớ: đảo ngữ sau trạng từ phủ định
box.intro: Khi một trạng từ phủ định hoặc hạn chế đứng đầu câu để nhấn mạnh, trợ động từ đứng trước chủ ngữ (như trong câu hỏi).

rows.subject: Rarely / Seldom / Never (before) + trợ động từ + S + V
rows.form: Rarely have employers complained so loudly.
rows.example: Never before has the pace of change been so fast.

rows.subject: Not only + trợ động từ + S + V, but ... also ...
rows.form: Not only does the model offer flexibility, but it also lacks protection.
rows.example: Vế sau but không đảo: it also lacks protection.

rows.subject: Hardly / Barely + had + S + V3 + when ...
rows.form: Hardly had the factory announced the robots when rumours spread.
rows.example: Dùng with had và when (không dùng than).

rows.subject: Little did + S + V
rows.form: Little did the board realise how serious the problem was.
rows.example: Little mang nghĩa phủ định: hầu như không biết.

box.note: Lỗi hay gặp: quên đảo (Rarely employers have...), đảo cả mệnh đề sau but, hoặc dùng than sau Hardly. Cấu trúc này trang trọng, chỉ dùng khi cần nhấn mạnh.

text: Supporters of automation make a case that is difficult to dismiss. Machines do not tire, take holidays or make arithmetic errors, so firms that adopt them can boost productivity without extending working hours. McKinsey estimates that up to 30 per cent of the hours worked in the United States could be automated by 2030. That figure explains why so many executives are eager to cut costs. In practice, the gains are often visible within months: an invoice that once took an hour to process now takes seconds. Few managers would willingly return to the old methods once they have seen the results.

Nor is the argument purely financial. Companies that streamline operations with cutting-edge systems tend to deliver faster, safer and more consistent services, and customers notice the difference. Seldom does a warehouse manager regret replacing a heavy lifting task with a machine, since labour-saving equipment removes precisely the work that injures backs and shortens careers.

Yet enthusiasm should be tempered. Automation is a double-edged sword: the very efficiency that lowers prices may also hollow out the occupations that once sustained entire towns. Little did the early adopters of factory robots imagine that the gains would be so unevenly shared. Economists remain divided on how quickly the benefits will spread. Not until policymakers intervene will the many reap the benefits that the few currently enjoy.

steps.title: Đọc
steps.heading: The risks of automation
steps.purpose: Đọc để tìm: tác giả lo ngại những rủi ro nào, và bằng chứng gì được dùng?
text: Critics of automation focus on what the headline statistics leave out. In the short term, it may well widen the inequality gap. McKinsey's analysis suggests that the two lowest wage groups are up to fourteen times more likely to have to switch occupations than the highest earners. Rarely does a cleaner or a cashier have the savings, or the time, to retrain for a new profession. The cost of failing is borne almost entirely by the individual.

Job security, once taken for granted in many industries, can no longer be assumed. Not only do employees fear losing their positions, but they also sense that their bargaining power is shrinking. A growing sense of insecurity now shapes how people spend, vote and plan their families. Employers rarely see this cost, yet it eventually reaches them in the form of lower morale and higher turnover.

There are subtler dangers too. Overreliance on automated tools can erode skills that took years to acquire; pilots, translators and radiologists all report that they practise fundamental techniques less than they once did. Never has a technology been so capable of imitating expertise. Seldom have organisations asked so few questions about what happens when it fails. If systems continue to put people out of work faster than new roles appear, existing protections will fall short of what society expects.

steps.sample: In my view, the two biggest risks are job insecurity and the loss of skills, and governments should respond with funded retraining.
steps.model: In my view, the two biggest risks are job insecurity and the loss of skills, and governments should respond with funded retraining. First, a growing sense of insecurity affects how people spend and plan their lives. Rarely do low-paid workers have the savings to retrain after they have been put out of work. Second, overreliance on automated tools can erode skills that took years to acquire. Not only does this harm individuals, but it also weakens whole industries. Existing protections fall short of what is needed, so I would argue that governments should pay for retraining and extend protection to gig workers.

steps.purpose: Đọc một bài mới dùng lại từ vựng và đảo ngữ của tuần: tác giả đề xuất chính sách gì?
text: Public debate about automation tends to swing between panic and complacency. Neither mood helps. The World Economic Forum expects 170 million jobs to be created and 92 million to disappear by 2030, which suggests a net gain. Yet a net figure says nothing about who gains and who loses.

Rarely do displaced workers move smoothly into the new roles. A welder who has been made redundant seldom finds that a vacancy in software testing matches his experience. It makes little difference how many such vacancies exist. Hardly had one cohort of workers been retrained when a new technology rendered their qualifications obsolete. That is why training must be continuous rather than occasional.

Governments therefore face a delicate task, and the margin for error is small. Not only must they encourage firms to invest in cutting-edge tools, but they must also ensure that the benefits are shared. Never has the case for a robust safety net been stronger, because without one a growing sense of insecurity will erode public trust in innovation itself.

The most credible policies combine three elements: affordable reskilling, protection for those between jobs, and honest information about which occupations are changing. Such a package is neither cheap nor quick, but it costs far less than the social consequences of inaction. Were societies to neglect any of these, the gap between winners and losers would only widen, and trust in institutions would follow it downwards.

steps.title: Đọc trước Sub 4
steps.heading: The way forward (preview)
steps.purpose: Đọc lướt để làm quen với tuần sau: tác giả đề xuất giải pháp gì?
text: What, then, should be done? The sensible answer is neither to resist technology nor to ignore its victims. Workers will need to reskill repeatedly, and lifelong learning must become a normal part of a career rather than an emergency measure. Societies that adapt to change quickly will fare better, but only if governments strike a balance between innovation and fairness and build a safety net for those who fall behind. This is a pressing issue, and the sooner policymakers act, the more they can mitigate the impact on the people least able to bear it.

In the end, a society is judged less by the machines it builds than by how fairly it treats the people those machines replace.
